dx: AIDS presenting with Pneumocystis pneumonia and Kaposi sarcoma
case: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-week history of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, and fever. He has lost 7 kg (15 lb) over 4 months and has never been tested for HIV. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse 112/min, respirations 28/min, and blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 87% on room air. Violaceous plaques are present on both shins and on the hard palate. Chest x-ray shows bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates. An HIV-1/2 antigen and antibody immunoassay is positive. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 62/mm3 (normal 500 to 1500), and plasma HIV-1 RNA is 280,000 copies/mL. Methenamine silver stain of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid shows cup-shaped cysts. Diagnosis: AIDS with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and Kaposi sarcoma.

questions.stem: Biopsy of a palatal plaque shows spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces that contain extravasated erythrocytes. Which of the following best explains the development of this lesion?
options: EBV infection of proliferating B lymphocytes
HHV-8 infection of endothelial-lineage cells
Bartonella henselae stimulation of capillary growth
HPV infection of squamous epithelial cells
approach: Recognize spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and red cell extravasation as Kaposi sarcoma.
Recall that Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor driven by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8).
Link its appearance to loss of T cell control of the virus in AIDS.
questions.why: Kaposi sarcoma is a tumor of endothelial-lineage (lymphatic-type) spindle cells infected with human herpesvirus 8, also called Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus. Viral proteins push the infected cells to divide and form leaky, slit-like vessels, which is why the lesions are purple and contain extravasated red cells. In a healthy host, cytotoxic T cells keep HHV-8 latent. When the CD4 count falls in AIDS, that control is lost and the tumor appears in skin, the mouth, the gut, and the lungs.
whyNot: EBV drives B cell proliferation and is linked to primary CNS lymphoma and oral hairy leukoplakia in AIDS. It does not cause a spindle cell vascular tumor.
Correct.

Bartonella henselae causes bacillary angiomatosis, which also forms red-purple skin lesions in AIDS. Its biopsy shows plump endothelial cells with neutrophils and clumps of bacteria on silver stain, and it responds to antibiotics.
High-risk HPV transforms squamous epithelium and causes anal and cervical carcinoma in people with HIV. It does not form vascular spindle cell lesions.

questions.stem: He recalls an illness 9 years ago, about 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse, with fever, sore throat, rash, and swollen lymph nodes that resolved within 2 weeks. He then felt well until this year. Which of the following best describes HIV activity during the years without symptoms?
options: Silent integrated provirus with no virion production
Viral clearance from blood with persistence in brain
Replication limited to genital mucosal epithelium
Ongoing replication in lymph nodes with CD4 loss
approach: Identify the remote illness as acute retroviral syndrome, the first stage of HIV infection.
Recall that the next stage, clinical latency, has no symptoms but is not virologically quiet.
Pick the option describing continuous replication in lymphoid tissue with slow CD4 decline.
questions.why: After acute infection, HIV enters a period of clinical latency that lasts about 8 to 10 years on average without treatment. The patient feels well, but billions of virions are made each day, mainly in lymph nodes and gut-associated lymphoid tissue, and CD4+ T cells are destroyed and replaced. Over the years the losses outpace replacement, the CD4 count falls, and opportunistic infections appear once it drops below 200/mm3. That threshold, or any AIDS-defining illness, defines AIDS.
whyNot: A latent provirus does exist in some resting memory T cells, and it is the reason HIV cannot be cured. Most infected cells, however, are actively making virus throughout the asymptomatic years.
Plasma viral load falls after acute infection to a set point, but the virus stays detectable in blood during latency. The brain is one reservoir, not the only site of virus.
Genital mucosa is a common entry site. Infected dendritic cells carry the virus to lymph nodes within days, so replication is not confined to the mucosa.
Correct.

topics: Acute retroviral syndrome and clinical latency

questions.stem: His partner tests positive for HIV. She gave birth to their daughter 6 weeks ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to determine whether the infant is infected?
options: HIV-1 RNA or DNA nucleic acid amplification test
HIV-1/2 antigen and antibody combination immunoassay
HIV-1/2 antibody differentiation immunoassay
CD4+ T-lymphocyte count and percentage
approach: Note that the mother is infected, so the infant received maternal IgG across the placenta.
Recall that maternal antibody can persist up to about 18 months and makes antibody-based tests positive in uninfected infants.
Choose a test that detects the virus itself: an HIV nucleic acid test.
questions.why: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta, so every infant born to a mother with HIV has anti-HIV antibodies at birth, infected or not. These antibodies can last up to about 18 months. Infants are therefore tested with a nucleic acid test that detects HIV RNA or proviral DNA, usually repeated at set ages in the first months. In adults, the antigen and antibody immunoassay is the screening test, a differentiation assay confirms HIV-1 versus HIV-2, the viral load measures replication, and the CD4 count stages disease.
whyNot: Correct.
This is the standard first screening test in adults and older children. In a young infant, its antibody component detects maternal IgG and gives a positive result even when the infant is uninfected.
This test confirms a reactive screen in adults and tells HIV-1 from HIV-2. It also detects antibody and is misleading in infants who carry maternal IgG.
The CD4 count stages immune damage in a person known to be infected. It cannot diagnose infection, and infant CD4 counts are normally much higher than adult values.

questions.stem: HIV proteins are synthesized in the cytosol of infected CD4+ T cells. Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells recognize peptides from these proteins presented on which of the following molecules?
options: HLA-DR alpha chain paired with a beta chain
HLA-DQ alpha chain paired with a beta chain
HLA-B heavy chain with beta2-microglobulin
HLA-DM alpha chain paired with a beta chain
approach: Identify the antigen as endogenous: viral protein made in the cytosol of the infected cell.
Recall that cytosolic peptides are loaded onto MHC class I in the endoplasmic reticulum and presented to CD8+ T cells.
Pick the class I molecule: HLA-A, -B, or -C heavy chain with beta2-microglobulin.
questions.why: Proteins made inside a cell, such as viral proteins, are cut by the proteasome, pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by TAP, and loaded onto MHC class I. Class I is an HLA-A, -B, or -C heavy chain paired with beta2-microglobulin, and it is found on all nucleated cells. CD8 binds class I, so cytotoxic T cells can find and kill any infected cell. MHC class II (HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR) has an alpha and a beta chain, is found mainly on antigen-presenting cells, and presents peptides from engulfed proteins to CD4+ T cells.
whyNot: HLA-DR is a class II molecule. It presents peptides from endocytosed proteins to CD4+ helper T cells, which do not carry CD8.
HLA-DQ is also class II and presents to CD4+ T cells. It is best known for its links to celiac disease (DQ2, DQ8).
Correct.
HLA-DM is a class II-like molecule inside endosomes that removes the invariant chain fragment (CLIP) so class II can load peptide. It does not present peptide on the cell surface.

topics: MHC class I versus class II

case: A 41-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her brother because of a 10-day history of headache and increasing confusion. Two days ago she developed weakness of her right arm and leg. She was diagnosed with HIV infection 6 years ago and stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago. Serum Toxoplasma gondii IgG was positive when HIV was diagnosed. Temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse 96/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg. She is oriented to person only, and there is right hemiparesis. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 74/mm3 (normal 500 to 1500). Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema in the basal ganglia and at the gray-white matter junction. Diagnosis: Toxoplasma encephalitis.

questions.stem: Her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 340/mm3 two years ago, just before she stopped antiretroviral therapy. At that count, which of the following opportunistic conditions was she most at risk of developing?
options: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex
Oral hairy leukoplakia
Cytomegalovirus retinitis
approach: Place 340/mm3 on the CD4 scale: below normal but above 200.
Recall the thresholds: Pneumocystis below 200, Toxoplasma below 100, CMV retinitis and MAC below 50.
Choose the condition that appears early, while the count is still above 200.
questions.why: Opportunistic infections in HIV follow the CD4 count closely. Conditions such as oral thrush, oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV), herpes zoster, and Kaposi sarcoma can appear while the count is still above 200/mm3. Pneumocystis pneumonia becomes common below 200, Toxoplasma encephalitis below 100, and CMV retinitis and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex below 50. Her current count of 74/mm3 fits the toxoplasmosis she has now.
whyNot: Pneumocystis pneumonia occurs mainly once the CD4 count falls below 200/mm3, which is why prophylaxis starts at that level.
Disseminated MAC occurs when the CD4 count is below 50/mm3, far lower than 340.
Correct.
CMV retinitis is a late complication that appears when the CD4 count falls below 50/mm3.

questions.stem: Her 26-year-old roommate, who has a normal immune system, acquires a primary Toxoplasma gondii infection during the same month. If the roommate develops symptoms, which of the following is most likely?
options: Fever with painless cervical lymphadenopathy
Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions
Hydrocephalus with diffuse brain calcifications
Bilateral diffuse interstitial pneumonitis
approach: Note the host: an immunocompetent adult with a new infection.
Recall that T cell immunity quickly turns tachyzoites into dormant tissue cysts, so most primary infections are silent.
Pick the usual symptomatic form in healthy adults: a mononucleosis-like illness with lymphadenopathy.
questions.why: Toxoplasma presentations depend on the host. Most healthy adults have no symptoms, and those who do usually have fever, fatigue, and painless cervical lymphadenopathy that looks like mononucleosis but is heterophile negative. Infection acquired in pregnancy can cross the placenta and cause chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications in the fetus. In AIDS with a CD4 count below 100/mm3, latent cysts reactivate and form multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions, as in this patient.
whyNot: Correct.
Multiple ring-enhancing lesions come from reactivated infection in severe T cell deficiency, as in this patient. A healthy host contains the parasite.
Hydrocephalus with diffuse calcifications is a sign of congenital toxoplasmosis, acquired across the placenta during fetal life.
Toxoplasma pneumonitis is rare and occurs in severely immunocompromised hosts. It is not an expected form in a healthy adult.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the source of the parasites now causing her brain lesions?
options: Sexual reproduction of the parasite within her brain
Recent ingestion of oocysts shed in cat feces
Spread to the brain from an intestinal sexual stage
Conversion of dormant bradyzoites in tissue cysts
approach: Note that she was Toxoplasma IgG positive years ago, so she already carried the parasite.
Recall that after primary infection, the parasite persists in brain and muscle as tissue cysts full of slowly dividing bradyzoites.
With CD4 loss, bradyzoites convert to rapidly dividing tachyzoites that destroy brain tissue.
questions.why: Toxoplasma gondii reproduces sexually only in the cat intestine, the definitive host, which sheds oocysts in its feces. Humans become infected by swallowing oocysts from soil or litter or tissue cysts in undercooked meat. In the human host the parasite spreads as tachyzoites and then, under T cell pressure, settles into tissue cysts that hold bradyzoites for life. In AIDS, loss of IFN-gamma-producing T cells lets bradyzoites convert back to tachyzoites, so most cases of Toxoplasma encephalitis are reactivations in people who were already seropositive.
whyNot: The sexual stage of Toxoplasma occurs only in the intestinal epithelium of cats. Humans are intermediate hosts and carry only asexual stages.
Ingested oocysts cause a new infection. She was already seropositive years earlier, so reactivation of an old infection is far more likely.
There is no intestinal sexual stage in humans. Only cats support the sexual cycle.
Correct.

topics: Reactivation of latent infection in AIDS

questions.stem: Her 38-year-old brother has had repeated sexual exposure to partners with HIV but remains uninfected. Genetic testing shows he is homozygous for a 32-base-pair deletion in the CCR5 gene. Which of the following viral proteins normally binds the host molecule that he lacks?
options: gp41 transmembrane protein
gp120 envelope protein
p24 capsid protein
p17 matrix protein
approach: Recognize that the CCR5 delta32 deletion prevents CCR5 from reaching the cell surface.
Recall the entry sequence: gp120 binds CD4, changes shape, and then binds a coreceptor (CCR5 or CXCR4).
Name the viral protein that binds the coreceptor: gp120.
questions.why: HIV entry starts when the envelope glycoprotein gp120 binds CD4. This shifts gp120 so it can bind a chemokine coreceptor, CCR5 on macrophages and memory T cells or CXCR4 on T cells. Coreceptor binding lets gp41 insert into the host membrane and fuse the viral and cell membranes. Most transmitted strains use CCR5, so people homozygous for the delta32 deletion, who have no CCR5 on their cells, strongly resist infection. Rare CXCR4-using strains can still infect them.
whyNot: gp41 carries out membrane fusion after gp120 has bound CD4 and the coreceptor. It does not bind CCR5 itself.
Correct.
p24 is the capsid protein encoded by gag. It is detected by fourth-generation screening tests and plays no part in receptor binding.
p17 is the gag-encoded matrix protein that lines the inside of the envelope. It does not bind host receptors.

dx: Reactivated pulmonary tuberculosis during TNF-alpha inhibitor and prednisone therapy for plaque psoriasis
case: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of cough, night sweats, and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. He has severe plaque psoriasis. Five months ago he began adalimumab, a monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha, and he has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for the past 2 months for a flare. A tuberculin skin test done for employment 10 years ago showed 14 mm of induration, and he did not complete treatment for latent infection. Temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse 98/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 128/80 mm Hg. Chest x-ray shows a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe. Sputum smear shows acid-fast bacilli, and culture grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Diagnosis: reactivation pulmonary tuberculosis during TNF-alpha inhibitor and glucocorticoid therapy.

questions.stem: His tuberculin skin test 10 years ago was read 48 to 72 hours after intradermal injection of purified protein derivative. Which of the following best explains the induration?
options: IgE-coated mast cells releasing histamine
Immune complexes fixing complement in venules
Antibody-dependent lysis of antigen-coated cells
Th1 cells recruiting and activating macrophages
approach: Note the timing: induration that peaks 48 to 72 hours after injection.
A delay of days points to a type IV (delayed-type) reaction carried out by memory T cells.
Memory Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, which recruits and activates macrophages, producing firm induration.
questions.why: The tuberculin test injects mycobacterial proteins into the skin. In a person previously sensitized, memory CD4+ Th1 cells recognize the antigen, release IFN-gamma and TNF, and recruit monocytes and macrophages, which takes 2 to 3 days. The result is a firm, raised area measured as induration, not redness. The same Th1 and macrophage response walls off M tuberculosis in caseating granulomas, where central necrosis is surrounded by epithelioid macrophages and Langhans giant cells. Sarcoidosis, by contrast, forms noncaseating granulomas.
whyNot: Histamine release from IgE-coated mast cells is type I hypersensitivity. It produces a wheal and flare within minutes and fades within hours.
Local immune complex deposition with complement is the Arthus reaction, a type III reaction. It peaks at about 4 to 10 hours and causes hemorrhagic necrosis, not delayed induration.
Antibody-dependent cell lysis is a type II mechanism directed at cell surface antigens. Tuberculin is a soluble protein injected into the dermis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following effects of his therapy most directly allowed the latent infection to reactivate?
options: Depletion of CD20-positive B cells
Loss of TNF-dependent granuloma integrity
Inhibition of calcineurin-dependent IL-2 transcription
Suppression of neutrophil production in the marrow
approach: Note his drugs: a TNF-alpha inhibitor plus a glucocorticoid.
Recall that latent M tuberculosis is held inside granulomas, and TNF keeps those granulomas organized.
Blocking TNF lets the granuloma break down and the bacilli multiply.
questions.why: In latent tuberculosis, bacilli survive inside granulomas built and maintained by Th1 cells and activated macrophages. TNF-alpha recruits cells, keeps macrophages activated, and holds the granuloma together. Blocking TNF with drugs such as adalimumab or infliximab lets granulomas loosen and the bacilli escape, which is why latent tuberculosis must be screened for and treated before these drugs are started. Prednisone adds to the risk by suppressing T cell and macrophage function.
whyNot: CD20 depletion is the action of rituximab. It removes B cells and is linked to hepatitis B reactivation, and B cells are not the main defense against M tuberculosis.
Correct.
Calcineurin inhibitors such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus block IL-2 transcription in T cells and are linked to Pneumocystis and viral infections. He is not taking one.
Glucocorticoids raise the neutrophil count, and TNF inhibitors rarely cause neutropenia. Neutropenia also predisposes to bacterial and fungal sepsis more than to tuberculosis.

questions.stem: Infected macrophages and dendritic cells secrete a cytokine that drives naive CD4+ T cells toward the helper subset needed to control M tuberculosis. Which of the following is this cytokine?
options: Interleukin-4
Interleukin-10
Interleukin-12
Transforming growth factor-beta
approach: Identify the helper subset that controls intracellular mycobacteria: Th1, which activates macrophages with IFN-gamma.
Recall which cytokine from antigen-presenting cells induces Th1 differentiation.
Answer IL-12.
questions.why: Each helper T cell subset is induced by a different cytokine signal. IL-12 from infected macrophages and dendritic cells drives Th1 cells, which make IFN-gamma to activate macrophages so they can kill intracellular bacteria such as M tuberculosis. IL-4 drives Th2 cells (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; IgE and eosinophils), IL-6 with TGF-beta drives Th17 cells (IL-17; neutrophils), and TGF-beta with IL-2 drives FOXP3-positive regulatory T cells. Inherited defects in the IL-12 or IFN-gamma receptor cause severe mycobacterial infections.
whyNot: IL-4 drives Th2 differentiation, which supports IgE class switching and eosinophils against helminths. It suppresses the Th1 response needed here.
IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine made by regulatory T cells and macrophages. It dampens macrophage activation rather than inducing Th1 cells.
Correct.
TGF-beta induces regulatory T cells, or Th17 cells when IL-6 is also present. Neither subset is the main defense against M tuberculosis.

topics: T helper subsets and their inducing cytokines

questions.stem: A complete blood count is obtained. Which of the following effects of his daily prednisone on the leukocyte differential is most likely?
options: Neutrophilia from demargination, with lymphopenia
Neutropenia from marrow suppression, with lymphocytosis
Eosinophilia from IL-5 release, with neutropenia
Lymphocytosis from thymic release, with eosinopenia
approach: Recall the glucocorticoid pattern on a blood count: neutrophils up; lymphocytes, eosinophils, and monocytes down.
Name the cause of the neutrophilia: cells that were stuck to vessel walls enter the circulating pool.
Choose the option that pairs demargination with lymphopenia.
questions.why: High cortisol, from stress, Cushing syndrome, or drugs such as prednisone, changes the blood count within hours. Neutrophils rise mainly because they detach from vessel walls (demargination), with added release from the marrow and slower exit into tissues. Lymphocytes and eosinophils fall because they are redistributed to lymphoid tissue and marrow and undergo apoptosis. Over time, high cortisol also shrinks the thymus. These changes are one reason glucocorticoids weaken T cell defense against intracellular organisms.
whyNot: Correct.
Glucocorticoids raise the neutrophil count and lower the lymphocyte count, the reverse of this pattern.
Glucocorticoids cause eosinopenia. That is why they are used in eosinophilic disorders and why low eosinophils are a clue to cortisol excess.
Glucocorticoids cause lymphopenia and thymic atrophy. They do not release T cells from the thymus.

topics: Glucocorticoid effects on the blood count

dx: Acute cellular rejection of a deceased-donor kidney transplant with CMV viremia
case: A 47-year-old woman comes to the transplant clinic because of fatigue and low-grade fever for 5 days. Seven weeks ago she received a deceased-donor kidney transplant for end-stage kidney disease from autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. The donor was cytomegalovirus (CMV) seropositive, and she was seronegative. Temperature is 38.0 °C (100.4 °F), pulse 92/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 146/90 mm Hg. The graft in the right iliac fossa is mildly tender. Serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL (normal 0.6 to 1.1), up from 1.2 mg/dL 2 weeks ago. Plasma CMV DNA is 45,000 IU/mL. Allograft biopsy shows a dense interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate with lymphocytes invading tubular epithelium; C4d staining of peritubular capillaries is negative. Diagnosis: acute T cell-mediated rejection with CMV viremia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of the biopsy findings?
options: Recipient T cells responding to donor HLA
Preformed recipient antibodies to donor HLA
Donor T cells responding to recipient HLA
Gradual intimal fibrosis of graft arteries
approach: Note the timing (7 weeks after transplant) and the biopsy: lymphocytes in the interstitium and tubules, C4d negative.
Weeks to months after transplant with tubulitis means acute cellular rejection.
In acute cellular rejection, the recipient's CD8+ and CD4+ T cells attack donor HLA on graft cells.
questions.why: Rejection is classified by timing and mechanism. Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes, from preformed antibodies against donor ABO or HLA antigens, and causes graft thrombosis. Acute rejection occurs over weeks to months: in the cellular form, recipient T cells that recognize donor HLA invade the interstitium and tubules, as here; in the antibody-mediated form, new donor-specific antibodies injure capillaries and leave C4d deposits. Chronic rejection develops over months to years as graft arteriosclerosis with intimal thickening and fibrosis. Graft-versus-host disease is the reverse direction, donor T cells attacking the host.
whyNot: Correct.
Preformed antibodies to donor HLA cause hyperacute rejection within minutes to hours of reperfusion, with thrombosis of graft vessels. This graft worked well for weeks.

Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue is graft-versus-host disease, which targets skin, liver, and gut. It follows hematopoietic stem cell transplants and lymphocyte-rich solid organs such as liver or small bowel, and it is very rare after kidney transplant.
Intimal fibrosis of graft arteries is chronic rejection, which develops over months to years. Her biopsy shows active lymphocytic infiltration at 7 weeks.

questions.stem: Before she was listed for a deceased-donor kidney, her two brothers were tested as possible living donors. Assuming no recombination within the HLA region, which of the following is the probability that a given brother inherited the same two HLA haplotypes that she did?
approach: Recall that the HLA genes on chromosome 6 are tightly linked and pass to a child as one haplotype from each parent.
Each sibling has a 1/2 chance of getting the same maternal haplotype and a 1/2 chance of getting the same paternal haplotype.
Multiply: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4, or 25%.
questions.why: The HLA genes sit close together on the short arm of chromosome 6, so each parent passes on a block of alleles called a haplotype. A child gets one haplotype from each parent, and both are expressed (codominant expression). For any sibling, the chance of sharing the same haplotype from the mother is 1/2, and from the father is 1/2, so the chance of a full match is 1/4. The chance of sharing exactly one haplotype is 1/2, and the chance of sharing none is 1/4. A fully matched sibling usually gives the best long-term graft survival.
whyNot: 6.25% is (1/4) squared. It would be the chance that two siblings are both full matches, not that one sibling is.
12.5% does not correspond to any standard haplotype outcome in two-parent inheritance.
Correct.
50% is the chance that a sibling shares exactly one haplotype (haploidentical), not both.

questions.stem: She had three pregnancies and received several blood transfusions while on dialysis. Before surgery, her serum was tested against lymphocytes from the donor. Which of the following results would have most strongly predicted hyperacute rejection?
options: Proliferation of her T cells with donor cells
Binding of her IgG to donor lymphocytes
One-allele mismatch at HLA-A with the donor
Anti-A antibodies in her serum with a group O donor
approach: Note her sensitizing events: pregnancies and transfusions expose a person to foreign HLA.
Recall that hyperacute rejection is caused by preformed antibodies that bind graft endothelium within minutes.
A positive crossmatch, her antibodies binding donor cells, detects those preformed antibodies.
questions.why: Pregnancy exposes a woman to paternal HLA on fetal cells, and transfusions and prior transplants expose a person to donor HLA. Both can leave preformed anti-HLA antibodies. If a graft carrying those HLA antigens is connected to the circulation, the antibodies bind its endothelium, fix complement, and cause thrombosis within minutes, which is hyperacute rejection. The crossmatch tests the recipient's serum against donor lymphocytes; a positive result is a contraindication to that transplant. HLA matching reduces later acute and chronic rejection.
whyNot: T cell proliferation in mixed culture (the mixed lymphocyte reaction) measures T cell recognition of donor HLA. T cells cause acute cellular rejection over weeks, not hyperacute rejection.
Correct.

Single HLA mismatches are common and are managed with immunosuppression. A mismatch raises the risk of later rejection but does not predict hyperacute rejection unless antibodies against that allele already exist.
A group O donor's cells carry neither A nor B antigen, so her anti-A antibodies have no target. ABO incompatibility would matter if the donor were group A.

questions.stem: Three weeks later she develops bloody diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain. Colonoscopy shows multiple shallow ulcers in the right colon. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on biopsy of an ulcer base?
options: Pseudomembranes of fibrin, mucus, and neutrophils
Multinucleated cells with ground-glass nuclei
Trophozoites containing ingested erythrocytes
Enlarged cells with intranuclear inclusions
approach: Note the setting: a transplant recipient on strong immunosuppression with CMV viremia from a seropositive donor.
CMV commonly causes colitis with ulcers in transplant and AIDS patients.
The diagnostic biopsy finding is large cells with an owl's eye intranuclear inclusion.
questions.why: Cytomegalovirus is a herpesvirus that remains latent after infection and causes disease when T cell immunity is weak. The highest risk after transplant is a seronegative recipient of an organ from a seropositive donor, as in this patient. CMV can cause fever, leukopenia, hepatitis, pneumonitis, retinitis, and colitis with ulcers. Infected cells, often endothelial or stromal cells at the ulcer base, become very large and show a dense intranuclear inclusion with a clear halo (owl's eye), sometimes with cytoplasmic inclusions too.
whyNot: Pseudomembranes of fibrin, mucus, and neutrophils describe Clostridioides difficile colitis, which usually follows antibiotic use and forms yellow plaques more than ulcers.
Multinucleated cells with ground-glass nuclei (molding, margination, multinucleation) are typical of herpes simplex virus, which more often causes esophagitis or proctitis.
Trophozoites with ingested red cells are the mark of Entamoeba histolytica, which forms flask-shaped ulcers after fecal-oral exposure.
Correct.

case: A 23-year-old woman is treated at an urgent care clinic for streptococcal pharyngitis with an intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G. As a child she had a mild rash while taking amoxicillin. Within 10 minutes of the injection, she develops generalized itching, hives, swelling of the lips, wheezing, and lightheadedness. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse 128/min, respirations 26/min, and blood pressure 78/42 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. There is diffuse urticaria, angioedema of the lips, and bilateral expiratory wheezing. She receives intramuscular epinephrine and intravenous fluids and improves within 30 minutes. Serum tryptase drawn 1 hour after onset is 38 ng/mL (normal less than 11.4). Diagnosis: penicillin anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A vasovagal reaction was considered at first because of her hypotension. Which of the following best explains why the elevated serum tryptase supports anaphylaxis instead?
options: Release from activated eosinophils
Degranulation of tissue mast cells
Leakage from hypoperfused hepatocytes
Secretion by activated neutrophils
approach: Recall that tryptase is a protease stored almost only in mast cell granules.
A rise in serum tryptase within 1 to 3 hours shows that mast cells degranulated.
Vasovagal syncope causes hypotension and bradycardia without mast cell activation, so tryptase stays normal.
questions.why: Anaphylaxis is a severe systemic type I reaction. Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils, which release histamine and other mediators, causing urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, and hypotension. Tryptase is stored almost only in mast cells and peaks in serum about 1 to 2 hours after onset, so a high level confirms mast cell activation. A vasovagal reaction causes hypotension with a slow pulse, pallor, and no hives or wheezing, and tryptase stays normal.
whyNot: Eosinophils release major basic protein and peroxidase, not tryptase. They arrive in the late phase and are not the source of an early tryptase rise.
Correct.
Hepatocytes do not store tryptase. Shock liver raises transaminases, not tryptase.
Neutrophils release myeloperoxidase and elastase. They do not contain meaningful amounts of tryptase.

questions.stem: Six hours later her wheezing returns despite an oral antihistamine. Mast cells activated earlier have synthesized lipid mediators from arachidonic acid. Which of the following mediators most likely causes this sustained bronchoconstriction?
options: Leukotriene D4
Leukotriene B4
Prostaglandin E2
Prostacyclin (PGI2)
approach: Note that an antihistamine did not help, so a mediator other than histamine is responsible.
Recall the 5-lipoxygenase products: LTB4 attracts neutrophils, while LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4 constrict bronchi and increase vascular permeability.
Pick the cysteinyl leukotriene.
questions.why: Mast cells release stored histamine within seconds and then make new lipid mediators from arachidonic acid over minutes to hours. The 5-lipoxygenase pathway produces LTB4, a neutrophil attractant, and the cysteinyl leukotrienes LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4, which are far more potent bronchoconstrictors than histamine and increase vascular permeability. The cyclooxygenase pathway produces prostaglandins and thromboxane. Antihistamines do not block leukotrienes, which is one reason bronchospasm can persist or return in a late phase.
whyNot: Correct.
LTB4 is a 5-lipoxygenase product, but its main action is neutrophil chemotaxis and adhesion. It does not cause strong bronchoconstriction.
PGE2 is a cyclooxygenase product that causes fever, pain, and vasodilation. In the airways it tends to relax smooth muscle.
Prostacyclin, made by endothelium, causes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation. It does not constrict bronchi.

questions.stem: A different patient receives high-dose intravenous penicillin for 2 weeks for endocarditis and develops anemia with spherocytes and a direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test positive for IgG. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this reaction?
options: IgE cross-linking on mast cells by penicillin
Drug-antibody complexes deposited in vessel walls
Drug-specific T cells releasing cytokines in tissue
IgG binding penicillin attached to red cells
approach: Note the findings: hemolysis with spherocytes and IgG on the red cell surface.
At high doses, penicillin binds red cell membranes and acts as a hapten.
IgG binds the drug-coated red cells, and splenic macrophages remove them: a type II reaction.
questions.why: The same drug can cause different types of hypersensitivity. Penicillin can cause anaphylaxis (type I, IgE on mast cells), hemolytic anemia (type II, IgG against drug bound to red cells, also seen with methyldopa through true autoantibodies), and serum sickness-like illness (type III, immune complexes). Topical drugs such as neomycin cause contact dermatitis (type IV, T cells). Here, high-dose penicillin coats the red cells, IgG binds the drug, and macrophages remove the coated cells, which explains the spherocytes and positive Coombs test.
whyNot: IgE cross-linking on mast cells is type I hypersensitivity, which causes anaphylaxis and urticaria within minutes. It does not cause hemolysis.
Immune complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity, which causes fever, rash, arthralgia, and nephritis. It does not coat red cells with IgG.
Drug-specific T cells cause type IV reactions such as contact dermatitis and some drug rashes. They do not produce a positive direct Coombs test.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her reaction began within minutes of the injection?
options: Preformed IgG forming complexes in vessels
Memory Th1 cells releasing interferon-gamma
IgE already bound to mast cells
Complement activation by IgM on endothelium
approach: Note her earlier exposure to amoxicillin, which can sensitize a person to penicillins.
Sensitization made penicillin-specific IgE, which sits on mast cell Fc epsilon receptors.
On re-exposure, the drug cross-links that IgE at once, so mediators are released within minutes.
questions.why: Hypersensitivity types differ by effector and timing. Type I needs prior sensitization: the first exposure produces IgE that binds Fc epsilon RI on mast cells, so on re-exposure the antigen cross-links bound IgE and mast cells degranulate within minutes. Type II (IgG or IgM against cell or matrix antigens) acts over hours to days, type III (immune complexes) appears about 1 to 2 weeks after a new antigen or 4 to 10 hours in a local Arthus reaction, and type IV (T cells) takes 48 to 72 hours.
whyNot: Immune complex reactions take hours locally and 1 to 2 weeks systemically. They cause vasculitis and complement consumption, not reactions within minutes.
Th1 cells drive delayed (type IV) reactions that need 2 to 3 days to recruit macrophages.
Correct.
Complement activation by IgM against endothelium occurs in hyperacute rejection of an ABO-incompatible graft. Penicillin anaphylaxis is driven by IgE, not IgM.

dx: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia in autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome
case: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of fatigue, pallor, and yellow eyes. He has had painless enlarged lymph nodes in the neck and axillae since age 3 years. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse 118/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg. He has scleral icterus, nontender lymphadenopathy, and a spleen palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin. Hemoglobin is 7.1 g/dL (normal 11.5 to 15.5), reticulocytes are 9% (normal 0.5 to 2.5), and total bilirubin is 3.4 mg/dL (normal 0.3 to 1.2), mostly unconjugated. Blood smear shows spherocytes. Direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG and negative for C3. CD4-negative, CD8-negative alpha-beta T cells are 8% of T cells (normal less than 2.5). A heterozygous FAS mutation is found. Diagnosis: warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia in autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the main mechanism of red cell destruction in this patient?
options: Oxidant precipitation of hemoglobin in red cells
Complement membrane attack complex lysis in vessels
Splenic macrophages removing IgG-coated red cells
Fragmentation of red cells by intravascular fibrin
approach: Note the direct antiglobulin test: IgG on red cells, no C3, with spherocytes.
IgG warm antibodies bind red cells at body temperature and do not fix complement well.
Splenic macrophages with Fc receptors bite off membrane (making spherocytes) or engulf the cells: extravascular hemolysis.
questions.why: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is caused by IgG autoantibodies that bind red cells at 37 °C (98.6 °F). Macrophages in the spleen bind the IgG through Fc receptors and remove pieces of membrane, turning the cells into spherocytes, or engulf them whole. It is linked to SLE, CLL, and other immune dysregulation such as ALPS. Cold agglutinin disease is different: IgM binds red cells in cool peripheral blood and fixes complement, giving a C3-positive Coombs test, acrocyanosis, and an association with Mycoplasma pneumoniae and EBV.
whyNot: Oxidant precipitation of hemoglobin forms Heinz bodies and bite cells in G6PD deficiency. The Coombs test would be negative.

Membrane attack complex lysis in vessels is the main mechanism in ABO transfusion reactions and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, and it contributes in cold agglutinin disease. His Coombs test is negative for C3.
Correct.
Fragmentation by fibrin strands produces schistocytes in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia such as TTP or HUS. The Coombs test would be negative.

topics: Warm versus cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia

questions.stem: The FAS mutation most likely causes his lymphadenopathy and autoimmunity by impairing which of the following?
options: Expression of tissue antigens by thymic medullary cells
Development of FOXP3-positive regulatory T cells
Release of perforin and granzymes by cytotoxic cells
Apoptosis of activated and self-reactive lymphocytes
approach: Recall that Fas (CD95) is a death receptor; binding Fas ligand activates caspases and apoptosis.
After an immune response, repeatedly activated lymphocytes kill each other through Fas, ending clonal expansion.
Without Fas, lymphocytes accumulate and self-reactive cells survive: lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and autoimmune cytopenias.
questions.why: Fas is a death receptor on lymphocytes. When it binds Fas ligand on another activated lymphocyte, it triggers the extrinsic apoptosis pathway through caspase 8. This activation-induced cell death shrinks lymphocyte clones after an infection is cleared and removes peripheral lymphocytes that recognize self antigen. In autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, FAS mutations block this pathway, so lymphocytes build up in nodes and spleen, unusual double-negative T cells appear, and autoantibodies cause hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia.
whyNot: Thymic expression of tissue antigens depends on AIRE. AIRE mutation causes autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1, not lymphoproliferation.
FOXP3 controls regulatory T cell development. FOXP3 mutation causes IPEX syndrome with enteropathy, diabetes, and eczema.
Perforin and granzyme release is a separate killing pathway. Defects in it cause familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: If his spleen were examined microscopically, IgG-coated red cells would be found trapped and ingested mainly in which of the following locations?
options: Splenic cords of the red pulp
Periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths
Germinal centers of white pulp follicles
Lumen of the central arterioles
approach: Trace splenic blood flow: central arteriole in the white pulp, then penicillar arterioles that open into the cords of the red pulp.
Red cells must squeeze from the cords through slits into the venous sinusoids.
Macrophages lining the cords catch rigid or antibody-coated red cells at this point.
questions.why: The spleen has white pulp and red pulp. White pulp is lymphoid tissue around central arterioles: the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath holds T cells, follicles hold B cells, and a marginal zone surrounds them. Branches of the central arteriole end in the red pulp, where blood flows openly into the splenic cords (of Billroth). Red cells must squeeze through narrow slits in the sinusoid walls to return to the veins, and cord macrophages remove cells that are old, rigid, or coated with IgG.
whyNot: Correct.
The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath is white pulp made of T cells. Red cells pass through central arterioles there but are not filtered or ingested.
Germinal centers are sites of B cell proliferation and selection. They do not filter red cells.
Red cells flow freely through central arterioles. Trapping occurs after blood leaves the arteriole and enters the cords.

questions.stem: Splenectomy is generally avoided in this syndrome. Loss of which of the following splenic functions poses the greatest threat to his life after splenectomy?
options: Removal of nuclear remnants from red cells
Clearance of encapsulated bacteria from blood
Storage of about one third of the platelet mass
Removal of aged red cells from the circulation
approach: List the spleen's jobs: filtering red cells, clearing bacteria, making IgM, and storing platelets.
Ask which loss can kill: overwhelming infection by encapsulated organisms.
Marginal zone B cells and macrophages clear opsonized encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae.
questions.why: The spleen filters blood. Red pulp macrophages remove aged red cells and pit out inclusions such as Howell-Jolly bodies. The marginal zone holds macrophages and B cells that respond quickly to polysaccharide capsules with IgM and remove opsonized bacteria from blood. The spleen also stores about one third of the platelets. After splenectomy, people are at lifelong risk of overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis, and this risk is higher in ALPS.
whyNot: Removal of nuclear remnants (Howell-Jolly bodies) is lost after splenectomy, but these inclusions are harmless. They serve only as a sign of absent splenic function.
Correct.
Loss of platelet storage causes a mild, usually harmless rise in the platelet count after splenectomy.
The liver and bone marrow macrophages take over removal of aged red cells, so this loss is not dangerous.

case: A 26-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of coughing up blood and passing dark urine. He smokes one pack of cigarettes daily. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse 104/min, respirations 22/min, and blood pressure 158/96 mm Hg. Crackles are heard over both lung bases. Serum creatinine is 3.8 mg/dL (normal 0.7 to 1.3); it was 0.9 mg/dL 1 month ago. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein and red blood cell casts. Chest x-ray shows bilateral patchy alveolar opacities. Serum anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are positive, and ANCA tests are negative. Kidney biopsy shows crescents in 80% of glomeruli. Diagnosis: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the target of the antibodies that injure both his lungs and his kidneys?
options: Alpha3 chain of type IV collagen
Myeloperoxidase in neutrophil granules
Proteinase 3 in neutrophil granules
Phospholipase A2 receptor on podocytes
approach: Note the combination: pulmonary hemorrhage plus rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with anti-GBM antibodies and negative ANCA.
Ask what antigen the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes share.
Both contain the noncollagenous domain of the alpha3 chain of type IV collagen.
questions.why: Goodpasture syndrome is a type II hypersensitivity in which IgG binds the noncollagenous (NC1) domain of the alpha3 chain of type IV collagen. This chain is found mainly in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, which explains hematuria with rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis and hemoptysis. The alveolar epitope is normally hidden, and smoking or other lung injury is thought to expose it, so pulmonary hemorrhage is more common in smokers. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG along the basement membrane.
whyNot: Correct.
Anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies (p-ANCA) occur in microscopic polyangiitis, which can also cause lung hemorrhage and crescentic nephritis. His ANCA tests are negative.
Anti-proteinase 3 antibodies (c-ANCA) occur in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, another pulmonary-renal syndrome. His ANCA tests are negative.
Antibodies to the phospholipase A2 receptor cause primary membranous nephropathy, which presents with nephrotic syndrome and does not affect the lungs.

questions.stem: HLA typing shows the allele most strongly associated with his disease. The same allele also increases the risk of which of the following?
options: Ankylosing spondylitis
Multiple sclerosis
Celiac disease
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
approach: Recall the HLA association of Goodpasture syndrome: HLA-DR2 (the DR15 split).
Recall which other disease is linked to DR2.
Multiple sclerosis shares the DR2 association.
questions.why: Many autoimmune diseases are linked to particular HLA alleles, likely because those alleles present certain self peptides well to T cells. HLA-DR2 (DR15) is associated with Goodpasture syndrome and multiple sclerosis. HLA-B27 is linked to ankylosing spondylitis and reactive and psoriatic arthritis, DQ2 and DQ8 to celiac disease, DR3 and DR4 to type 1 diabetes, and DR4 to rheumatoid arthritis. An HLA association raises risk but does not cause disease by itself.
whyNot: Ankylosing spondylitis is linked to HLA-B27, a class I allele, not to DR2.
Correct.
Celiac disease is linked to HLA-DQ2 and DQ8, which present gluten-derived peptides to T cells.
Type 1 diabetes is linked to DR3 and DR4. DR2 (DR15) is actually associated with protection from type 1 diabetes.

questions.stem: Which of the following immunofluorescence findings is most likely on his kidney biopsy, with its correct interpretation?
options: Granular IgG and C3, from circulating immune complexes
Mesangial IgA, from deposited IgA-containing complexes
Linear IgG, from antibody bound to a fixed antigen
Scant immunoglobulin, from ANCA-driven neutrophil injury
approach: Identify the mechanism: antibody binding directly to a structural antigen in the basement membrane (type II).
An antigen spread evenly along the membrane gives an even, linear stain.
Immune complexes from the blood (type III) deposit in clumps and give a granular stain.
questions.why: Immunofluorescence helps classify immune-mediated kidney disease. In type II hypersensitivity, antibody binds an antigen that is part of the tissue itself; in anti-GBM disease the antigen lines the whole basement membrane, so IgG staining is smooth and linear. In type III hypersensitivity, antigen-antibody complexes form in the blood or in place and lodge in clumps, giving a lumpy granular pattern, as in lupus nephritis and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. ANCA vasculitis shows little or no immunoglobulin and is called pauci-immune.
whyNot: Granular IgG and C3 is the pattern of type III immune complex disease, such as lupus nephritis or poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Mesangial IgA deposits are seen in IgA nephropathy and IgA vasculitis, which do not cause lung hemorrhage with anti-GBM antibodies.
Correct.
Scant immunoglobulin (pauci-immune) staining is seen in ANCA-associated vasculitis. His ANCA tests are negative and anti-GBM antibodies are present.

topics: Type II versus type III hypersensitivity

questions.stem: Antibody bound to the glomerular basement membrane activates the classical complement pathway. Which of the following complement fragments most directly recruits neutrophils into the glomeruli?
options: C3b
C4b
C5b-9
C5a
approach: Recall that bound IgG activates C1 and the classical pathway, generating C3 and C5 convertases.
Sort the fragments by job: opsonin, anaphylatoxin and chemoattractant, or membrane attack complex.
C5a is the strongest complement chemoattractant for neutrophils.
questions.why: Complement fragments have distinct jobs. C3b coats targets so phagocytes can bind them (opsonization) and helps clear immune complexes. C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that make mast cells release histamine, and C5a is also a potent chemoattractant that brings neutrophils to the site. C5b through C9 form the membrane attack complex, which punches holes in cell membranes. In anti-GBM disease, neutrophils drawn in by C5a release proteases and oxidants that break the basement membrane and lead to crescents.
whyNot: C3b is the main opsonin. It helps phagocytes bind targets but does not itself draw neutrophils to the site.
C4b is part of the classical C3 convertase (C4b2a). It has no chemotactic role.
C5b-9 is the membrane attack complex, which lyses cells and can injure glomerular cells directly. It does not attract neutrophils.
Correct.

case: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen toward evening. She also has difficulty climbing stairs and tires while chewing meat. Vital signs are within normal limits. Sustained upward gaze for 60 seconds produces worsening bilateral ptosis, which improves after an ice pack is held over the eyelids for 2 minutes. Proximal limb strength is 4/5 and decreases with repeated testing. Deep tendon reflexes and sensation are normal. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz shows a decremental response. Serum acetylcholine receptor-binding antibodies are positive. CT scan of the chest shows a 5-cm mass in the anterior mediastinum. Diagnosis: myasthenia gravis with thymoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her weakness increases with repeated muscle use?
options: Loss of lower motor neurons in the anterior horn
Reduced calcium entry at presynaptic nerve terminals
Excess acetylcholine from blocked acetylcholinesterase
Too few receptors to reach threshold as release falls
approach: Note the pattern: weakness that worsens with use and a decremental response to repeated stimulation.
Recall that the amount of acetylcholine released falls with each impulse in a train, even in healthy people.
With fewer receptors, end-plate potentials drop below threshold as release declines, so more fibers fail.
questions.why: Myasthenia gravis is a type II hypersensitivity in which antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (or MuSK) reduce working receptors without killing the muscle cell. The antibodies cross-link receptors so they are internalized, activate complement that damages the end-plate folds, and can block acetylcholine binding. Normally the end-plate potential far exceeds threshold, so the normal fall in acetylcholine release during repeated firing does not matter. With fewer receptors, that safety margin is lost, more fibers fail with each impulse, and weakness and the decrement worsen with use. Rest restores release, and cooling slows acetylcholinesterase, which is why the ice pack helps.
whyNot: Loss of lower motor neurons, as in ALS, causes fasciculations, atrophy, and weakness that does not fluctuate with use.

Reduced presynaptic calcium entry is the defect in Lambert-Eaton syndrome, caused by antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels. Strength there improves briefly with repeated effort, and reflexes are reduced.
Excess acetylcholine from cholinesterase blockade occurs in organophosphate poisoning, which causes cholinergic signs such as miosis, salivation, and bronchorrhea.
Correct.

questions.stem: The mass lies behind the manubrium, anterior to the great vessels. Which of the following lesions also characteristically arises in this mediastinal compartment?
options: Schwannoma of an intercostal nerve
Esophageal duplication cyst
Mature cystic teratoma
Bronchogenic cyst
approach: Place the thymus: anterior and superior mediastinum, behind the manubrium and in front of the great vessels and pericardium.
Recall the classic anterior mediastinal masses: thymoma, teratoma and other germ cell tumors, lymphoma, and retrosternal thyroid.
Choose the germ cell tumor.
questions.why: The adult thymus lies in the anterior and superior mediastinum, behind the manubrium and in front of the left brachiocephalic vein, aortic arch, and pericardium. Masses in this compartment are classically thymoma, teratoma and other germ cell tumors, lymphoma, and retrosternal goiter. Thymoma is the most common anterior mediastinal mass in adults and is the one linked to myasthenia gravis and other paraneoplastic autoimmune disorders. Middle mediastinal masses include bronchogenic cysts and lymph nodes, and posterior masses include nerve sheath tumors.
whyNot: Schwannomas and other neurogenic tumors arise from intercostal nerves or sympathetic chain in the posterior mediastinum, along the spine.
Esophageal duplication cysts arise along the esophagus in the middle or posterior mediastinum.
Correct.
Bronchogenic cysts arise from the foregut near the trachea and carina, in the middle mediastinum.

questions.stem: Neoplastic epithelial cells in thymomas often fail to express AIRE, which may help explain the autoimmunity seen with these tumors. A germline loss-of-function mutation in AIRE causes a syndrome with which of the following combinations?
options: Enteropathy, type 1 diabetes, and eczematous dermatitis
Candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency
Lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias
Hypocalcemia, conotruncal defects, absent thymus
approach: Recall what AIRE does: drives medullary thymic epithelial cells to express tissue-specific self antigens.
Without AIRE, T cells that recognize these antigens escape negative selection.
The result is autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency.
questions.why: AIRE is a transcription regulator in medullary thymic epithelial cells. It switches on genes for proteins normally made only in other organs, such as parathyroid and adrenal proteins, so developing T cells that react strongly to them are deleted. Loss of AIRE causes autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APECED), with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency. The candidiasis comes from autoantibodies that neutralize IL-17 and IL-22, cytokines that defend against Candida. Thymomas that lack AIRE can produce a similar loss of tolerance.
whyNot: Enteropathy, type 1 diabetes, and eczema make up IPEX syndrome, caused by FOXP3 mutation and loss of regulatory T cells.
Correct.
Lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and autoimmune cytopenias describe autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome from FAS mutation.
Hypocalcemia, conotruncal heart defects, and an absent thymus describe 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome, a developmental defect of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.

questions.stem: She asks whether removing her thymus will weaken her immune defenses. Which of the following best explains why thymectomy at her age causes little loss of T cell immunity?
options: Peripheral T cells persist and divide
Bone marrow assumes thymic selection of T cells
Lymph nodes take over production of new T cells
B cells assume the functions of helper T cells
approach: Recall that the thymus is most active before puberty and then involutes, with fat replacing much of the lymphoid tissue.
By adulthood, the T cell pool is already formed and is kept up mainly by division of existing peripheral T cells.
Removing the thymus therefore leaves established T cell immunity largely intact.
questions.why: The thymus is largest relative to body size in early childhood and begins to involute after puberty, as adipose tissue replaces much of the cortex and medulla. Thymic output of new T cells falls steadily with age. The adult T cell pool is kept up mainly by long-lived naive and memory T cells that slowly divide in the periphery in response to cytokines such as IL-7 and IL-15. For this reason, thymectomy in an adult causes little measurable immune deficit, while absence of the thymus in infancy, as in DiGeorge syndrome, causes severe T cell deficiency.
whyNot: Correct.
Positive and negative selection of T cells require thymic epithelium. Bone marrow makes T cell precursors but cannot select T cells.
Lymph nodes house and activate mature T cells but do not produce new T cells from precursors.
B cells cannot perform helper T cell functions. They depend on T cell help for class switching and affinity maturation.

topics: Maintenance of the peripheral T cell pool

dx: Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis
case: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of hand joint pain, a facial rash that worsens with sun exposure, and ankle swelling. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse 92/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 152/94 mm Hg. Physical examination shows malar erythema sparing the nasolabial folds, tender wrists and finger joints without deformity, and ankle edema. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL (normal 12 to 16), platelet count is 92,000/mm3 (normal 150,000 to 400,000), and serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL (normal 0.6 to 1.1). Urinalysis shows 3+ protein and red blood cell casts. Antinuclear and anti-dsDNA antibodies are positive. Serum C3 is 48 mg/dL (normal 90 to 180), and C4 is 6 mg/dL (normal 10 to 40). Kidney biopsy shows diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with wire-loop lesions. Diagnosis: systemic lupus erythematosus with diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains how her antinuclear autoantibodies arise?
options: Cross-reactive antibodies to streptococcal antigens
Poor clearance of apoptotic nuclear debris
Drug-induced antibodies directed against histones
Inherited loss of FOXP3-positive regulatory T cells
approach: Recall that the antigens in SLE are nuclear: DNA, histones, and ribonucleoproteins.
These antigens become exposed when apoptotic cells are not cleared promptly.
Persistent nuclear debris activates self-reactive B and T cells, producing antinuclear antibodies and immune complexes.
questions.why: In SLE, nuclear material from dying cells is cleared too slowly, for example because of inherited deficiency of early complement proteins (C1q, C2, C4) or defects in phagocyte uptake. Nucleic acids in this debris stimulate Toll-like receptors and type I interferon, and self-reactive B cells make antibodies to DNA and nuclear proteins. These antibodies form immune complexes that deposit in kidneys, skin, joints, and serosa (type III). ANA is very sensitive, anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific, anti-dsDNA tracks nephritis activity, and C3 and C4 fall during flares as complement is consumed.
whyNot: Cross-reaction with streptococcal antigens (molecular mimicry) causes acute rheumatic fever. It does not produce antinuclear antibodies.
Correct.
Drug-induced lupus, from drugs such as hydralazine or procainamide, produces anti-histone antibodies and rarely affects the kidneys. She takes no such drug, and anti-dsDNA points to idiopathic SLE.
Loss of FOXP3-positive regulatory T cells causes IPEX syndrome in infant boys, with enteropathy, diabetes, and eczema.

questions.stem: Three years later she has a second-trimester pregnancy loss and then a deep venous thrombosis of the left leg. Which of the following coagulation findings is most likely?
options: Prolonged PT that corrects after vitamin K is given
Prolonged aPTT that corrects after mixing with normal plasma
Low fibrinogen with a markedly elevated D-dimer level
Prolonged aPTT that does not correct after mixing
approach: Recognize pregnancy loss plus venous thrombosis in a woman with SLE as antiphospholipid syndrome.
Recall that the lupus anticoagulant binds phospholipid in the test tube and prolongs the aPTT.
Because it is an inhibitor, adding normal plasma does not correct the prolonged aPTT.
questions.why: Antiphospholipid syndrome occurs alone or with SLE and causes venous and arterial thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss. The antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I) promote clotting in the body. In the laboratory, lupus anticoagulant binds the phospholipid used in clotting tests, so the aPTT is prolonged. A mixing study does not correct it, which shows an inhibitor and not a missing factor. Anticardiolipin antibodies can also cause a false-positive syphilis (VDRL) test.
whyNot: A prolonged PT that corrects with vitamin K reflects deficiency of factors II, VII, IX, and X from malabsorption or warfarin. It causes bleeding, not thrombosis.
An aPTT that corrects with mixing points to a factor deficiency, such as hemophilia A or B. Factor deficiency causes bleeding.
Low fibrinogen with high D-dimer is the pattern of disseminated intravascular coagulation, which is consumptive and usually causes bleeding along with clotting.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her serum complement levels?
options: Classical pathway consumption by immune complexes
Alternative pathway activation that spares C4
Unchecked C1 activity from C1 inhibitor deficiency
Inherited deficiency of the terminal components
approach: Note that both C3 and C4 are low.
C4 is used only by the classical and lectin pathways; C3 is used by all three.
Immune complexes activate the classical pathway, consuming C4 and C3 together.
questions.why: Complement levels show which pathway is being used up. Immune complexes in active SLE bind C1q and activate the classical pathway, which consumes C4 and C2 and then C3, so both C3 and C4 are low; levels rise toward normal when the flare is controlled. In poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, the alternative pathway is activated, so C3 is low while C4 stays normal. In hereditary angioedema, C1 inhibitor deficiency lets C1 cleave C4 unchecked, so C4 is low while C3 is normal.
whyNot: Correct.
Alternative pathway activation lowers C3 but leaves C4 normal, as in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Her C4 is low.
C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angioedema) lowers C4 but leaves C3 normal, and it causes swelling without urticaria.
Terminal component (C5 to C9) deficiency raises the risk of Neisseria infections. It does not lower C3 and C4.

questions.stem: Helper T cells that support her anti-dsDNA response escaped deletion during development. Which of the following best describes where and how T cells with high affinity for self antigen are normally deleted?
options: Thymic cortex, for failing to bind self-MHC
Bone marrow, by receptor editing of light chains
Thymic medulla, by strong self-antigen binding
Germinal centers, by somatic hypermutation
approach: Recall the order of thymic maturation: double-negative, then double-positive thymocytes in the cortex, then single-positive cells in the medulla.
Positive selection in the cortex keeps cells that bind self-MHC weakly.
Negative selection in the medulla deletes cells that bind self-peptide on MHC strongly.
questions.why: Thymocytes enter the cortex as CD4-negative, CD8-negative (double-negative) cells, rearrange their T cell receptor, and become double-positive. In the cortex, cortical epithelial cells test them for weak binding to self-MHC; cells that fail die by neglect, which is positive selection. Survivors become CD4 or CD8 single-positive and move to the medulla, where medullary epithelial cells (using AIRE) and dendritic cells display self antigens. Cells that bind these strongly undergo apoptosis, which is negative selection. Escapees are normally held in check by peripheral tolerance.
whyNot: Death in the cortex for failing to bind self-MHC is the failure of positive selection. It removes useless T cells, not self-reactive ones.
Receptor editing in the bone marrow rescues self-reactive B cells by changing their light chain. It does not apply to T cells.
Correct.
Somatic hypermutation in germinal centers raises B cell antibody affinity. It is a process of B cells, not a T cell deletion mechanism.

dx: Polyarteritis nodosa associated with chronic hepatitis B
case: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of fever, muscle aches, a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss, and abdominal pain that begins about 30 minutes after meals. One week ago she developed weakness of her right foot. She has untreated chronic hepatitis B. Temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), pulse 96/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 168/100 mm Hg. Examination shows livedo reticularis, tender nodules on both calves, and right foot drop. The lungs are clear. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 88 mm/h (normal 0 to 20), and serum creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL (normal 0.6 to 1.1). HBsAg is positive, and ANCA tests are negative. Angiography shows multiple microaneurysms of the renal and mesenteric arteries. Biopsy of a calf nodule shows necrotizing inflammation of a medium-sized artery. Diagnosis: polyarteritis nodosa associated with chronic hepatitis B.

questions.stem: Biopsies taken from several of her affected arteries at the same time would most likely show which of the following?
options: Granulomas with giant cells along the internal elastic lamina
Necrotizing granulomas involving small vessels of the lung
Concentric onion-skin intimal thickening without inflammation
Segmental fibrinoid necrosis at varied stages of healing
approach: Identify polyarteritis nodosa: a necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries, ANCA negative, sparing the lungs.
Recall its key histologic feature: segmental transmural fibrinoid necrosis with neutrophils.
Because lesions start at different times, acute necrosis, healing, and fibrotic scars appear side by side.
questions.why: Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis of small and medium-sized muscular arteries, often linked to hepatitis B through immune complexes of HBsAg and antibody. It affects the kidneys, gut, nerves, and skin and characteristically spares the lungs, and ANCA is negative. Lesions are segmental and often at branch points: acute ones show transmural fibrinoid necrosis with neutrophils, while older ones show fibrous thickening of the wall. Different stages coexist in the same patient. Weakened walls form microaneurysms, and narrowed lumens cause infarcts such as her mesenteric ischemia, foot drop from mononeuritis multiplex, and renin-mediated hypertension.
whyNot: Granulomas with giant cells along a fragmented internal elastic lamina describe giant cell arteritis or Takayasu arteritis, which affect large arteries.
Necrotizing granulomas with small-vessel vasculitis in the lung describe granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which is c-ANCA positive. Her lungs are spared and ANCA is negative.
Onion-skin intimal thickening is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis of malignant hypertension, a change in arterioles without vasculitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Circulating complexes of hepatitis B surface antigen and antibody deposit in her arteries. A similar systemic immune complex reaction can follow treatment with a chimeric monoclonal antibody. Which of the following presentations is most typical of that reaction?
options: Hives and wheezing within 30 minutes of the first infusion
Fever, rash, arthralgia, and low C3 about 10 days later
Hemolysis with a positive direct Coombs test after 3 days
Vesicular dermatitis at the infusion site after 48 hours
approach: Recognize the systemic immune complex reaction to a foreign protein as serum sickness (type III).
Antibody to the foreign protein takes about 1 to 2 weeks to form, then complexes form while antigen is still present.
Complexes deposit in vessels, joints, and kidneys and consume complement: fever, rash, arthralgia, proteinuria, low C3.
questions.why: Serum sickness is a systemic type III reaction. A foreign protein, such as the mouse portion of a chimeric monoclonal antibody or antivenom, triggers antibody production over about 1 to 2 weeks. Antibody then meets the antigen still in the blood, forming complexes that lodge in small vessels, synovium, and glomeruli and activate complement. This produces fever, urticarial rash, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, proteinuria, and low complement levels, and it subsides as the antigen is cleared. The Arthus reaction is the local version, a necrotizing vasculitis at an injection site that peaks within hours in a person who already has high antibody levels.
whyNot: Hives and wheezing within minutes are a type I or infusion reaction, mediated by IgE or direct mast cell activation, not immune complexes.
Correct.
Hemolysis with a positive Coombs test is a type II reaction, from antibody binding drug-coated or self antigens on red cells.
Vesicular dermatitis after 48 hours at a contact site is a type IV (T cell) reaction, as in contact dermatitis from topical neomycin.

topics: Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction

questions.stem: Neutrophils are abundant in her acutely inflamed arteries. In a child with a CD18 mutation (leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1), neutrophils could not have entered these vessel walls. Which of the following interactions is defective in that child?
options: Sialyl-Lewis X binding to E-selectin
PECAM-1 binding to PECAM-1
LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1
C5a binding to its neutrophil receptor
approach: Recall the steps of extravasation: rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins), diapedesis (PECAM-1), and chemotaxis.
CD18 is the beta2 subunit shared by the leukocyte integrins LFA-1 and Mac-1.
Without CD18, LFA-1 cannot bind ICAM-1, so neutrophils roll but cannot stop and exit.
questions.why: Neutrophils leave the blood in steps. TNF and IL-1 from the inflamed site make endothelium express E-selectin and P-selectin, which bind sialyl-Lewis X on neutrophils and make them roll. Chemokines such as IL-8 then activate beta2 integrins (LFA-1 and Mac-1, which share CD18) to bind ICAM-1 tightly, stopping the cell. The neutrophil crawls between endothelial cells using PECAM-1 and follows gradients of C5a, LTB4, and IL-8 to the target. In leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, CD18 is missing, so neutrophils cannot adhere firmly, causing neutrophilia, delayed umbilical cord separation, and infections without pus.
whyNot: Sialyl-Lewis X binding to selectins mediates rolling. Its loss causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2, from a defect in fucose metabolism, not a CD18 mutation.
PECAM-1 binding mediates diapedesis between endothelial cells. It does not involve CD18.
Correct.
C5a binding its G protein-coupled receptor directs chemotaxis. The receptor is not CD18, so chemotactic signaling is intact in this disorder.

questions.stem: Her fever and weight loss reflect high levels of IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha. Which of the following iron study patterns is most likely?
options: Low serum iron and high ferritin
High transferrin and low ferritin
High serum iron and low hepcidin
High serum iron and high transferrin saturation
approach: Recall the acute phase response: IL-6 makes the liver produce more CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, ferritin, and hepcidin, and less albumin and transferrin.
Hepcidin degrades ferroportin, trapping iron in macrophages and enterocytes.
Serum iron falls while stored iron (ferritin) rises: the pattern of anemia of chronic disease.
questions.why: IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha drive the acute phase response. They cause fever by inducing prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus, which raises the temperature set point. IL-6 makes hepatocytes produce more CRP, fibrinogen (which raises the ESR), serum amyloid A, ferritin, and hepcidin, and less albumin and transferrin. Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, the iron exporter, so iron is trapped in macrophages and gut cells. Serum iron falls, ferritin rises, and transferrin is low to normal, the pattern of anemia of chronic disease.
whyNot: Correct.
High transferrin with low ferritin is the pattern of iron deficiency. Inflammation lowers transferrin and raises ferritin.
Inflammation raises hepcidin, which lowers serum iron. Low hepcidin with high iron is the pattern of hereditary hemochromatosis.
High iron with high transferrin saturation indicates iron overload. Inflammation lowers serum iron and saturation.
